title: WorkOS Pricing: What Each Connection Costs (2026)
summary: WorkOS pricing is based on per-connection fees that vary by plan. You'll find the SSO cost structure and how billing scales as your connections increase.
body_markdown:
## Frequently asked questions


The forecast and the spreadsheet leave a few questions open, and each answer below ends at the same place: WorkOS's own pricing page, read on the day you sign.


Is WorkOS free for small projects? Starting is cheap, but check the page for what's free today, because terms there can change. The bill that matters begins when an enterprise customer connects SSO or a directory.


A side project with many users and no enterprise buyers can stay inexpensive. A small product with a few large customers can't.


Does WorkOS charge extra for Directory Sync? Plan on it, and model it as its own line. SSO and Directory Sync are separate features, so a customer who wants both may count as more than one billable item.


Confirm on the page how each is counted. If you forecast only SSO and the buyer's IT team asks for provisioning, your number will be too low.


### Can I pass WorkOS connection fees on to my customers?


Yes, as a pricing decision of your own, not as a WorkOS feature. Nothing here stops you from putting SSO and directory sync in an enterprise tier or charging a setup fee.


That's usually the cleanest way to keep your margin from shrinking as connections grow, but it only works if your contracts say so before the first customer connects.


Does WorkOS offer discounts for annual or high-volume contracts? Ask, but don't build the forecast on a discount you haven't seen in writing. The pricing page shows list terms.


Anything beyond that comes from a sales conversation, so use list price as your planning number. A discount then becomes upside, and you won't be caught short if it never arrives.


How often does WorkOS change its pricing? Often enough that you should re-read the page before each forecast review, and I can't give you a schedule.


Treat any figure you copied into a spreadsheet as dated. Record the day you checked it next to the number, so whoever inherits the model knows how stale it might be.
